div.head: Scene
div.stage: SCENE,

A Garden, on one side the Vestibule of Calas' House —on the other a Pavilion with a Door—at the back a handsome Iron Gate practicable—on the outside a low practicable Town Rampart—the Suburbs and a beautiful Country beyond them—Garden Seats, banks of Flower &c. over the Stage—the Pavilion is beautifully shaded with Garden Trees and flowering Shrubs—the whole Scene very gay.—Time Sunrise.
MUSIC EXPRESSIVE OF BIRDS AND MORNING.

As the Curtain rises, Laurence appears in the distance, traversing the Angles of the Rampart—he carries a bundle on his stick over his shoulder—passes the Walls, and at length appears on the outside of the Garden Gate, which he tries but cannot open—Music ceases.

sp.speaker: Laurence.
sp.p: BLESS us! the bolt won't open—I dare say that's because its lock'd, and the gate's fast because nobody sha'nt go in without ringing the bell—
Jacob! papa Jacob! its only me—what have you lock'd the gate for?

sp.speaker: Jacob,
sp.p: Coming! coming! I haven't finish'd my toilet—
Who in the name of wonder rings our bell? Monsieur Calas don't expect any one —ah—why its Laurence, I do declare.

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: Yes, its me papa Jacob—I'm here.

sp.speaker: Jacob.
sp.p: Indeed!

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: Yes, indeed, in propria persona, as our curate says.

sp.speaker: Jacob.
sp.p: Impossible!

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: It may be impossible, but its very true for all that, papa Jacob, so open the gate, for I bring good news.

sp.speaker: Jacob.
sp.p: Good news! only let me unlock the gate.

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: The sooner the better, for I long to shake hands with you, and give my dear Jeanette, your daughter that is, and my wife that will be, such a kiss!
And how are you, and how is Jeanette?

sp.speaker: Jacob.
sp.p: She's much as all girls are, who expect every day to be married; she laughs, sings, and talks all day.

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: Does she? dear me! love has made me quite different —I'm as melancholy as an owl by daylight. I haven't seen Jeanette for three months, and that's a long while for a youth of my insensibility, as our curate calls it.

sp.speaker: Jacob.
sp.p: You're an honest youth, I believe, and as you're absence was occasioned by your attention to a sick relation, my daughter loves you the better for it. Your master, the counsellor, has spoken highly of you, while you were away, and when he comes from Bourdeaux to marry our young lady, you shall, on the same day, marry my daughter.

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: Pretty soul! loves me better for three month's absence! if I had staid six, how fond she'd ha' been; and cou'd I have made it a twelvemonth, there'd have been no end to her delight—well, well, as our curate says, I begin to see the aurora of my happiness.

sp.speaker: Jacob.
sp.p: But what is the good news you tell of?

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: Good news! Oh, true! in the first place, my poor dear uncle is dead.

sp.speaker: Jacob.
sp.p: Poor man! in the flower of his age.

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: Yes, thank fate, he was seventy-seven —a sad thing when a man has lived so long, to die at last—left me his little all—and the doctors said, if he hadn't had a combregation of disorders, and a fit of perplexity, they'd have made a fine cure of him, and saved me all the money he has left behind him.

sp.speaker: Jacob.
sp.p: Great pity! great pity! any more news?

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: Eh! no, none—but that my master, the counsellor, will be here directly—he desired me to mention it the very first moment I arrived, and you see I have obeyed my orders.

sp.speaker: Jacob.
sp.p: Good lad!

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: Tell Mr. Calas, said he, and all his good family, I shall be in their arms, and at the feet of my dear Ma'amselle Pauline, within half an hour of your arrival.

sp.speaker: Jacob.
sp.p: That is good news, indeed! I must let 'em all know—Jeannette! Jeannette!

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: Coming, father!

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: Dear me! that's her voice sure enough—how my heart beats!—call her again, if you please, papa Jacob.

sp.speaker: Jacob.
sp.p: Jeannette! Jeannette!

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: Stay a moment, father; I'm not half drest, would you have me come this figure?

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: Not half drest! call her again papa Jacob, tell her to come directly.

div.stage: Enter Jeannette tying on her Bonnet, Laurence hides behind Jacob.

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: La! father, whats the matter? is the house on fire?

sp.speaker: Jacob.
sp.p: Eh—why there is as a body may say a sort of flame that—

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: Flame! where? where, father?

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: Here, lilly on of my first love— here, rosebud of my recollections, as our curate says, the flame that burns in the first floor of my heart has got so much ahead, that the roof of my attic affections will tumble in, unless the little fireman, Cupid, brings you as the engine to distinguish my conflagration.

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: Ah, ha, ha, ha, ha! how glad I am to be sure.

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: Ah ha, ha, ha, ha, ha, ha!—so am I.

sp.speaker: Jacob.
sp.p: Now what the devil are you both so glad of?

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: Why father, my dream's out—it was such a good one.

sp.speaker: Jacob.
sp.p: Indeed!

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: Dreaming of me?

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: Yes—I thought the first thing I should see this morning was—a white cow.

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: Me! a white cow!

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: Twice! I dream'd it twice.

sp.speaker: Jacob.
sp.p: And—it should have been a calf—well, well, pay the rest of your compliments while I call up the family. How happy it is your master should arrive when they stand so much in need of consolation.

div.stage: [Exit into the Vestibule.

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: Consolation! dear me! Jeannette, what does he mean, on so happy a day as this to talk of any thing so cruel as consolation.

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: O dear!

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: What does he talk about consolation for, its a mournful word, as our curate says, you shall have no consolation when we're married, not a bit—has any thing happen'd to your good master or his dear family?

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: Such things!—our good master—don't mention it again, but our good master has enemies—aye, here in Toulouse too.

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: Well, so have I—and its partly your fault, for double-jointed Peter the blacksmith was hammerous of you, as our curate says, and is so angry about our intended wedding, that he threaten'd to ram a red hot horse-shoe down my throat on the day of my marriage.

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: Only to think of his impertinence, what an affront.

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: But I shan't swallow it, if he was twice as big— tho' he can thump an anvil, I can thrash in a barn, and my flail shall match his sledge whenever he likes.

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: Well but Laurence—

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: I'll give him consolation, and merrily too.

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: Now Laurence, you're such another man.

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: And is he Monsieur Calas' enemy—I only wish he was—he's a red hot spark, but I'll knock the wind out of his bellows, blow me if I don't.

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: No no, our master's enemy is the Capitoul, the first ma—magistrate I think they call him of the city, and there's another, one Mr. Ambroise, not a bit honester than the judge—and then there's our young master, Mr. Antoine—

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: What is he an enemy?

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: To no one but himself—I'm afraid he's a—a little mad—and what's worse, he's in love.

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: Ah that accounts for his being mad—why before I was in love with you I was—

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: Nonsense!

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: No, I wasn't—

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: Its that Ambroise I tell you has somehow bewitch'd him—he neither sleeps eats nor drinks.

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: How thin he must have grown.

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: He walks by himself, talks to himself, and looks so miserable that all the family is in desolation to find out—

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: Who has bewitch'd him?—it can't be goody Grizzleton the cowkeeper's widow, because—

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: Because she's dead you goose—no, it must be Ambroise, he comes like a sprite, and always tries to avoid us when he visits young master, never looks up, always makes such low bows, and smiles with such a grin that—ah! talk of—

div.stage: Sees Ambroise, who has been coming over the Rampart during her speech.

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: Talk of the devil as our curate says and—bless me! that's a great likeness—

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.p: Of the devil, my good friend?

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: No, no—sir, of double jointed Peter, whom I mean to wallop.

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.p: Jeannette, why this distance?

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: Its a very good distance, sir.

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: Or if you don't think so sir, she can come further.

div.stage: (Pulling her towards himself.)

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.p: I know you are not my friend, but if I should prove the purity of my intentions, the difficulty—

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: It would be a great difficulty as you say, sir.

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.p: Indeed.

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: Is that Mr. Ambro—

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: Hush! yes—did you ever see such a—

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: No—he's like nothing but himself.

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.p: I wait the commands of your young master.

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: I'll tell him, sir. Laurence, I won't leave you alone with him.

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: No don't. Good morning, sir—You dream'd of a white cow, Jeannette, and if you hadn't seen me first—

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: Come, come along!

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: Dreams go by contraries, as our curate says, and that gentleman's so like a black bull, that double jointed Peter himself cou'dn't—

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: Come along, I tell you!

div.stage: [They go chattering into the house.

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.p: I am suspected, but I care not—their suspicions come too late, and vengeance is at hand—his sending for me is beyond my hopes—it will enable me to finish the plan I have formed. His father little thinks, that by his boasted integrity, in discovering and chasing from this city a party of, what he called, contraband traders, he ruined all my prospects:—unable, publicly, to reveal my wrongs, my revenge shall be secret, but dreadfully effective! Antoine loves, and loves to madness—his father will never consent to his marriage in a family so opposite to his principles of every sort.—But Antoine has gone too far, he has pledged his patrimony, he has involved himself in their power, and must be exposed, or marry one, whose character, when known, will expose him more:—yes—the marriage shall be performed in secret to-night, and to-morrow the shame of my enemy's family shall be proclaimed to the whole city—but he comes.

div.stage: Enter Antoine Calas.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Ambroise! my friend! I have sent for you in a moment of despair. I have more reason than ever to be convinced my family will never consent to my union with Hortensia: it will be impossible ever for me to repay the debts I have contracted, by the seduction of play, with her friends.—I am dying with love for her— remorse for my follies, and fear of discovery—and what! —what will become of me!

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.p: Hortensia is ready to proffer you her hand—the altar waits to receive you.—political and religious opinions, at present, divide your families, but your union will reconcile all.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: I have sworn to my father, and—

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.p: And love has shewn the folly of your oath. Marry—let it be secret for awhile—her fortune will pay your debts, and your family will consent, when there is no remedy.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: You are heavily indebted to my father.

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.p: Which your acknowledgements on paper here will pay—

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: And nothing—

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.p: But the fortune of Hortensia will exonerate you —to night you must decide—

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: I will!—Gaming—illicit passion!—what shall remedy—

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.p: All will be forgiven, if you renounce the errors of your faith. The altar which I now go to illuminate— the temple where you shall receive the hand of your adored—the forgiveness, your father must perforce accord —and the rejoicing of all your friends to-morrow—

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: To-morrow! well, let it come—I have well considered —go—I love Hortensia dearly—dearly as the vital spark which warms my bosom. I have made her father a proposal—take it—should he accept it, all may be well—should he reject it—

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.p: Hortensia will be doomed to a convent; and your disgrace as a broken gamester inevitable! her character is already lost—redeem what you have to answer for, and—

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: And, who was my seducer?—but no more—carry my letter—bring back the answer of Hortensia's father, and—

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.p: And if not favorable—

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: I know my path—I am the first branch of the family of Calas, who has stained it with dishonor, but I will not be the first who fears to repay the offence with his life!—Aye, Ambroise, with his life!

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.p: Antoine! my friend!

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Begone—you have the letter, an answer quick, quick!

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.p: You are in the power of the father of Hortensia.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: My heart is in the power of his daughter, but no man's honour is in the power of even Hortensia's father— go, go, go!

I am lost—what noise!—let me endeavour to avoid my family—the kind regards of my father and—the tears—the tears of a mother! Oh God! I am in folly! I am in love!—the eyes of her I love are firebrands—but the tears of a mother! and such a mother!—the greatest calamity a son can suffer is to dread the tears of her who first clasp'd him to a parent's bosom; —they come!—I can neither support their kindness nor their anger.

div.stage: [Exit into the Pavilion.
Enter from the House, Calas, Madame Calas, Pauline, Jacob, Laurence, and Jeannette.

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: See, see, my dear husband! our son flies at our approach

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: And why, mamma!

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: Alas, your father and I are equally ignorant.

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: I see the reason—master! sir! Monsieur Calas! look, there lurks that Mr Ambroise— that wicked man that turns our young master's head.

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: Jeannette, I forbid you so to speak of one we scarcely know, but who is honour'd by the friendship of my son.—
Let us not estrange a heart by reproaches, which is already too much disposed to forget us.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: Do not believe it dear father, my brother has never, never ceas'd to love you.

sp.speaker: Jacob.
sp.p: Shall I command him to attend you, sir?

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: O no—no commands—they would make him think he was summon'd before a judge—his own heart will direct him when to seek his father—the arrival of my friend Edward gives me a hope that his influence may prove a remedy.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: That it will I'm certain—Edward is so good, so manly, so full of dignity—that for all he's a counsellor he does every thing I bid him, and I'm sure will be the friend of my dear dear brother.

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: Dear, good Pauline—there is yet hope, my husband—

sp.speaker: Jacob.
sp.p: Yes, Madame; and there will be a féte too, I hope, to welcome Mr. Edward.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: Yes; and a ball mamma, if you'll permit it.

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: Certainly: I give up my authority to you for the day.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: Thanky'e, my dear mamma! Now, Jacob, Jeannette, Laurence!

sp.speaker: All.
sp.p: Here we are, Miss, ready to receive your orders.

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: I'll go and welcome Edward.

div.stage: (A servant brings his hat and cane, he goes out.)

sp.speaker: Jacob.
sp.p: Jeannette, bring my hat and cane, that I may attend our master; and, dye hear, make up the bed in the pavilion for Laurence.

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: Do; and then I shall hear the birds sing in the morning, without waking any body.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: And don't forget to send in all the neighbours.

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: No, miss; except Peter the farrier, and—

div.stage: (Sings—“Come along, Jeannette.”—Exit with her.)

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: Pauline, I depend on you for all—prepare to receive a worthy man; his mature age, talents, and integrity, will insure your happiness.—Go, I would speak with your brother.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: Yes, mamma; Edward is all you say, and if he is not, I wish I may never be married! and, in that case, dear me, what a disappointment it would be to both of us.

div.stage: [Exit.

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: Dear girl!—she is happy, and deserves to be so.—Ah, were her brother but as kind! he loves and fears his father; but his mother—fear cannot mingle with his love for her—he comes.

div.stage: Enter Antoine from the Pavilion.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: My mother! I am conscious that I have given offence, but do not reproach me—you can say nothing more severe than what my heart has already charged me with.

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: Cruel young man—our tears are the only reproaches we shall make you: our hearts are broken— you were our only hope, which is now extinguished.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: As my hopes are! yet am I a monster to cause those tears, which return upon my heart like a devouring flame! I would give my life! yes, every drop of my blood! to turn a single pang from my father, or from the kindest, best of mothers!

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: Indeed! my son! my dearest son!

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Beloved! dearest! yet my conduct—

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: Has never estranged from you the regard of your parents.—Oh, give them your confidence— tell them ere too late.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Tell them!—Oh wait!—patience—to day will finish, and develop all.

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: To-day!

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: To-day my trouble, and your uncertainty, will finish —and for ever.

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: For ever! dear, dear, son!

div.stage: Enter Pauline.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: Mamma, mamma! Edward is come!—My dear brother, I'm sure you're quite as glad as I am, and need not be half so much afraid to own it.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: I am rejoiced, indeed, dear sister.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: And you'll stay and see the fête for my sake?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: For thine, and for the sake of my dear, dear mother.

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: For me! then we shall yet be happy.

div.stage: [Exit with Pauline into the house.
Enter Ambroise.

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.p: Antoine: I bring you such an answer as I feared.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: There is no hope then?

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.p: None.—To-morrow Hortensia bids adieu to the world: a cloister will shut up that unfortunate, and bury her youth, beauty, and the remembrance, she must bitterly feel, of having loved Antoine.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Hortensia!

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.p: Would you become her executioner, at the vernal age of seventeen! embellished with all the virtues, all the graces—burning with chastest fires for yourself! would you consign her, living, to the tomb? Had you seen her bless you at my departure—she! the victim! who dies, while you abandon her—a word would restore her to life and happiness.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: And me—to—oh! to renounce my parents, my religion—all, all!

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.p: But your honour—the altar waits your vows— her life depends on it—her father will become the friend of yours—your debts of honour will be extinguished, and—

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Go! go!—haste—the sacrifice is ready, and this night shall consummate all—I go to write once more— send me a messenger.

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.p: And when we meet again 'twill be for happiness.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Heaven send it—haste! send me a messenger—

Now an instant of reflection—my patrimony I have lost at play—my love is given to the daughter of a house which has ever been my father's greatest enemy—Hortensia loves me—but there are horrid doubts—her character— and—yes—I—I love her—the confidence of my family is gone—reared with the greatest care—I've no excuse. I see my crime and have no remedy—even Ambroise I suspect —he would seduce, and then expose me—come then, foul demon! tempter!—How my brain revolves!— my father!

div.stage: Enter Calas, Madame Calas, Edward, Pauline, Jeannette, Laurence, &c. &c.

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: Dear Edward, take my daughter.

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: Yes, the heart of Pauline and her parents are in unison.

sp.speaker: Edward.
sp.p: May I believe—dearest Pauline?

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: I always am of the same opinion as ma and pa.

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: What an obedient hussey it is.

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: Well, and so are all girls, when they're bid.

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: My son, will you not welcome Edward?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Welcome him! yes! dear father!

div.stage: (embracing Edward.)

sp.speaker: Mde Calas.
sp.p: His heart is not changed.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Edward! you are going to be united to my dear sister, my parents love you —be you to them a kind, an affectionate son—the happiness of Pauline and of all my family is my first desire—

div.stage: (retires as if overcome)

sp.p: They're all coming to welcome Mr. Edward, and prepare for the fête.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: Yes mamma, they're all coming.

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: My son!

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Allow me to retire—father! at your knees—

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: In my arms!

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: And you will forgive—

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: Forgive! who! what!

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: Oh, why did I attempt to have a fête, when—

sp.speaker: Jacob.
sp.p: The company's coming.

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: Yes, they're all come.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Edward! comfort, console my parents: you have acted rightly! may your lot, as it must, be happy.

div.stage: [Exit abruptly.

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: My son!

sp.speaker: Jacob.
sp.p: Fear not, madam; I'll not lose sight of him

div.stage: [Exit.

sp.stage: Guests enter, and a dance takes place. At the end of it, Madam Calas says to Jacob:—
sp.p: How have you left my son?

sp.speaker: Jacob.
sp.p: Composed, madam; quite composed:—he has written a short letter, and insisted on giving it himself to a porter.

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: Our friends are departing.

div.stage: The company go—Servants light them out with flambeaux —The family go into the house, and when the stage is clear, Antoine enters.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: The noise of festivity has ceased: darkness has succeeded the brilliancy of mirth: there wants no light to avoid the path of dishonor. Yes,

that shall be the place—I shall have no witnesses and I have written and sent a confession to the magistrate, which will act, I hope, as a warning for others Mother!— father!—friends! adieu!—my faults will be—no matter— Ambroise will be disappointed—my deceivers will be deceived—and those who loved me—farewell—farewell, for ever!

div.stage: [Exit into the pavilion.
(The family re-enter from seeing the company out.)

sp.speaker: Jacob.
sp.p: Every body's gone—its very late.

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: Mr. Edward's apartment is quite ready.

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: Come, my children, to-morrow will exceed today in pleasure; your marriage will take place, and we shall all be happy. Jacob, shut the doors.

div.stage: Calas affectionately takes leave of Edward, who embraces Pauline, then leads Madame Calas into the house, and Calas conducts his daughter.

sp.speaker: Jacob.
sp.p: Now, Jeannette, you must make up a bed for our friend here.

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: No thanky'e, I'm so happy, I'm sure I shan't be able to sleep at all.

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: Nonsense!

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: Nonsense, what for, I wonder!

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: Because, I won't marry any man who doesn't go to sleep every night; so, shut the gates, father, and I'll go look to the bed.

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: And I'll go with you.

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: Lord, you'll be of no use—go help my father to lock the great gate.

div.stage: [Exit into the pavilion.
Laurence goes with Jacob to lock the gate, when a scream is heard from the pavilion.

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: O, lud! what's the matter—don't be frighten'd, papa, Jacob.

sp.speaker: Jacob.
sp.p: Frightened! when did you see me—O, dear! it was the voice of my daughter!

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: Oh, father! father!

sp.speaker: Jacob & Lau.
sp.p: Eh! what!

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: A man murdered! assassinated!

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: Oh, mercy! oh, lud, oh, lud!

div.stage: Jeannette runs into the vestibule to give the alarm. Ambroise, who has been watching, enters—Jacob and Laurence go into the pavilion.

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.p: A man assassinated in the house of my enemy— this may produce more food for my revenge—let us observe.

div.stage: [retires.
Calas, Madame Calas, Edward, Jacob, Laurence, Jeannette, and Attendants enter. Jacob and Laurence from the pavilion.

sp.speaker: Jacob.
sp.p: 'Tis our young master! he is murdered!

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: A murder! in my house!

sp.speaker: Jacob.
sp.p: Madame! do not go, for the love of Heaven!

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: Why, in Heaven's name?

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: Mother! mother! my brother is not in his room!

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: I feared, I feared it all!—let me go—
sp.stage: Calas enters in great agony from the pavilion, interupts Madame Calas as she is going to the spot, who understanding his distress, exclaims:—
sp.p: My son! my son then is no more!

div.stage: (falls into the arms of Jacob.)

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: My brother!

div.stage: She is caught by her father—Jeannette is held by Laurence. Ambroise appears observing all that passes— Jacob watches him. A picture is formed, and the act-drop falls.

div.head: Scene
div.stage: SCENE,

The Interior of the Vestibule, looking towards the Garden, as in Act I. Doors on each side, the Pavilion seen in a reversed position, as from the house. As the Drop rises the town clock is heard to strike two—a lamp hangs from the ceiling of the Vestibule.
Madame Calas discovered seated, and attended by Pauline and Jeannette. Calas in front of them, comes forward as if listening, looks around, and speaks.—

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: I tremble at the slightest noise that disturbs the silence, and augments the horror of the night. If from yon ramparts, or any of the neighbouring houses, they should have seen us remove the body of my unfortunate son, all will be lost!

Silence!—dear wife, and thou, my daughter, suppress your grief, tremble to awake suspicion. Alas! you know not the severe law which, in this country, sentences to the last disgrace, the corpse of each unfortunate who has been guilty of self-destruction; —his bleeding remains must be given to the public executioner, ignominiously dragged forth by an infuriated mob, and disgracefully cast out without the rites of sepulture.

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: My son!

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: Let us at least save his remains from such horror —let us hide his error, and let our affection for his memory arm us with strength to conceal our despair.

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: Yes, yes, my husband—we will be silent— we will cease to weep.

div.stage: (In an agony of tears.)

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: Unfortunate brother! Oh, what misfortune! what misery!

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: My father!

div.stage: Enter Jacob.

sp.speaker: Jacob.
sp.p: Hush! the clock has strucken two,—in the silence of the night the smallest noise will be overheard.

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: Did Edward depart without being perceived?

sp.speaker: Jacob.
sp.p: He did—I concealed my light while he and Laurence went out together, and I am certain that no one pass'd at that moment.

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: Why did Laurence go?

sp.speaker: Jacob.
sp.p: To accompany his master, to be sure, in such a night.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: In such a night could Edward quit us—

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: In a moment so cruel?

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: Do not accuse him: he is gone secretly to find the pastor of our church, and concert with him on the means of performing the last duties to our lost son.

sp.speaker: Jacob.
sp.p: I gave Mr. Edward a key, to let himself in on his return. Had not Madame better retire to rest?

sp.speaker: Mde Calas.
sp.p: Is not the corpse of my son within that chamber?

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: For that reason, pray retire; leave us to watch —Pauline, persuade your mother.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: Pray, dearest, dearest mother—
sp.stage: (she permits herself, after some difficulty, to be led out between the daughter and husband.)

sp.speaker: Jacob.
sp.p: I had forgot—stay here, Jeannette, while I—

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: Father! would you leave me—here, and alone!

sp.speaker: Jacob.
sp.p: Why not? I must watch what passes without.

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: No, father; stay here, or take me with you—I am so frightened to be so near the murdered body of— hush—what was that?

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: A-hem!

sp.speaker: Jacob.
sp.p: Hem!

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: Some one calls.

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: Papa, Jacob! are you there?

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: Ah, 'tis Laurence!

sp.speaker: Jacob.
sp.p: This way; where's your master, and what news have you?—whisper.

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: No good, papa Jacob: oh, if you did but know—

sp.speaker: Jean. & Jacob.
sp.p: What! what!

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: Why, as our curate says—

sp.speaker: Jacob.
sp.p: Confound your curate—speak out.

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: Aye, do, dear Laurence, speak out.

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: Speak out! why, just now you bid me whisper— well, its all over the city, already—and worse than that—

sp.speaker: Jacob.
sp.p: Worse!

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: Yes; they say it was an assassin killed the young man.

sp.speaker: Jacob & Jeannette.
sp.p: An assassin! who?

div.stage: (a distant noise heard.)

sp.speaker: Jean. & Lau.
sp.p: O lud ha' mercy! what noise was that?

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: Let us call Monsieur Calas.

sp.speaker: Jacob.
sp.p: No—why alarm him now?

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: I hear voices in the street—ah! some one enters.

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: I left my master on the watch—perhaps—

sp.speaker: Jacob.
sp.p: Yes, 'tis Mr. Edward—

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: Jacob! Jeannette! where is Monsieur Calas?

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: Ah, sir—how alarmed you seem!

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: I ask you where is your master?

sp.speaker: Jacob.
sp.p: With his wife and daughter.

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: He is yet to learn then—and—ah, how shall I inform him!

sp.speaker: Jacob.
sp.p: Is it possible that what Laurence says is true— do they think our young master fell by other hands than his own?

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: O yes, and worse—worst of all—they suspect—

sp.speaker: All.
sp.p: Who? who?

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: Listen!—no, no, I cannot yet bring my tongue to—
listen—my friends—you— you love your good master, and would do much to save his life, if it were menaced?

sp.speaker: Jacob.
sp.p: Much!

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: Every thing!

sp.speaker: Jacob.
sp.p: We would lose our own.

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: You haven't an instant to spare then. You Jeannette, inform your young lady, without letting others observe you, that I would speak to her alone.

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: Yes, sir.

div.stage: [Exit at the door on the right.

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: You, Jacob, watch the gate next the street—if people assemble, give intelligence.

sp.speaker: Jacob.
sp.p: On the instant.

div.stage: [Exit by the garden.

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: You, Laurence, pass quietly to the town-hall— observe what goes forward, and return to inform me.

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: Mightn't I take Jeannette with me, for fear she should be seen?

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: Fly, blockhead.
Dreadful prejudice!— unfortunate Calas, sixty years of life without reproach have been spent in vain—surrounded by enemies, a single word has proved sufficient to prosecute thee.
Ah! dear Pauline.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: Edward! why did you not come to the apartment of my parents? come, come, and assist my feeble efforts to sustain their courage.

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: Their courage! alas, Pauline! you are yet far from knowing the added misery, the greatness of the peril which yet awaits them, which yet hangs over the head of your worthy father.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: My father! say what added misery! what peril?

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: If the savage acclamations of a misguided multitude were not about to inform you, you would not, could not credit your Edward's dreadful story, nay I even yet doubt whether or not my senses have deceived me. The hatred and revenge of fiends whom your father's upright conduct has offended, are at the most unnatural height, for sure it is unnatural! horrible! when to secure a victim, they do not hesitate to accuse a father of the murder of his son!

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: What say'st thou? gracious Heaven!

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: My master a murderer! and of his son!

div.stage: (Covers her face with her hands, retires by degrees, weeping.

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: Dearest Pauline, the softness of your nature, the innocence of your heart, your youth, and the prudence of your parents have placed, till this day, a veil between your ideas and the cruel prejudices which exist among men, misled by error;—never could you have thought them capable of such injustice;—you tremble, and well you may—yes, Pauline, it is said, nay more, it is believed that your brother was about to relinquish the faith of his ancesters to obtain the hand of her he loved, and that he was immolated by his father to prevent the sacrifice.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: God!

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: Yes, it is to him only you can appeal against a calumny so monstrous.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: A father immolate his son! the crime is impossible —but he will justify himself.

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: He is lost unless we can snatch him from the base ruffians of this city, from his accusers, and even from his judges—dear Pauline, I depend on you, and on your courage, on the empire which your filial love gives you over the heart of your father, to preserve him from the dreadful effects of this fatal evil.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: O do but speak, what shall I do, what will I not try to accomplish.

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: You must persuade your father to quit his home, to fly far from Toulouse.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: Now?—in the middle of the night?

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: This very moment—but in uniting our efforts for this necessary purpose, let us spare him the knowledge of this terrible accusation—the thought would be his death.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: And my mother too—Oh, Edward, how my heart bleeds for her!—father! brother! Edward! do not, do not you forsake us.

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: We lose time—come.
What now?

sp.speaker: Jacob.
sp.p: Ah, my dear Mr. Edward— we are lost—all's over—the street is full of people, they watch our house—they whisper—they are agitated and confused; voices speak of our master, of murder, and revenge, nor do I think they will long refrain from forcing their way in.

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: They dare not unless sanctioned by the magistrates —let us profit of this delay to—
sp.stage: (A tremendous crash as if windows were driven in, accompanied by a hurried shout of Calas! Calas!—the family all rush in from the door on the right.)

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: Great Heaven! what tumult!

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: My daughter!

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: Hold! stay! do not show yourself.

sp.speaker: Calas & Mde. Calas.
sp.p: Edward!

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: Not show myself!—what mean you?

sp.speaker: Edw. & Paul.
sp.p: Silence! caution!

sp.speaker: Jacob.
sp.p: Be ruled, sir, or we are lost.

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: Fear not—he will never resign to their rage, the corse of his hapless son!

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: Resign it! never—no, not with my life!

div.stage: (more noise is heard—Jeannette enters.)

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: They break down all before them, and are forcing their way.
There are are soldiers too, who bid them retire.

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: Our misfortune is at its height then—they come, armed with the law, to take useless vengeance on a hapless suicide!—did you see the pastor?

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: No, my friend; and your misfortune surpasses your imagination—I know not what demon discovered and reported the death of your son; but hatred, ignorance, and fury, have armed even the magistrates of the town against you.

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: I feared it—yes; their barbarity would expose on a scaffold, the corpse of my unhappy son; merely, for the sake of overwhelming a poor old man, his wife, and daughter, with ignominy and disgrace, in addition to the cruel weight of affliction, which already bows him down.

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: Alas! you do not know all yet.

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: Not all!!!

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: No: you stand on a horrid precipice, and flight is your only resource: at Bourdeux, my family will open an asylum for you.—I will conduct you to their arms, and never quit you. I am now your son, the betrothed husband of Pauline, and our fate is inseparable.—Come then, my friend, my father, favored by the night, we may pass disguised through the throng, or by way of yonder ramparts.

sp.speaker: Jean & Jacob.
sp.p: Yes; come, come.

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: Me! fly!

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: Quit his house!—who will watch over the remains of my boy? who will supplicate the magistrates to have pity on him, if not his father?

sp.speaker: Jacob & Jean.
sp.p: We will, madame; we will.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: My father; if ever you loved your daughter— if ever you loved my mother, or your dear lost child, be guided by my Edward.
sp.stage: (they all kneel to him, except Madame Calas.)

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: What cause? what mystery?

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: Another instant, and you are lost for ever!

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: My husband lost!

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: His life! his life's at stake!

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: His life: oh, let him go then—I too will kneel—

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: Explain, or on this spot—

div.stage: Enter Laurence running.

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: Monsieur Calas! Monsieur Calas! oh, there you are, and I have lost so much breath, that—

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: Are they at hand?

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: They're come to arrest, poor dear Mr. Calas— they're close at my heels—judges, clerks, soldiers—

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: He is insane—his fears have driven him mad.

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: Believe him—

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: He speaks the truth—

sp.speaker: Jacob.
sp.p: My master! my poor master!

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: 'Twill be too late—

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: What's to be done?

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: What's to be done? submit us to the will of Heaven, and pray, that it will deign to soften the hearts of my enemies, in favor of my son's remains.
In the name of the Capitoul, open!

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: Jacob, open the gates.
sp.stage: (Jacob looks at Edward, he and Pauline seem to forbid. Jeannette stops her father, and Madame Calas clings to her husband, who after a moment's pause, says firmly:)
sp.p: Jacob, I have commanded, and will be obeyed.

sp.speaker: Jacob.
sp.p: And for the first time unwillingly.

div.stage: [Exit.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: Edward, my father must—he must be told.

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: 'Tis too late—let us hope—perhaps, they will not dare accuse him

sp.speaker: Calas
sp.p: Dearest wife, have better resolution—whatever they think of us, they will not be proof against so heartbreaking a spectacle
sp.stage: (throws open a door, where there is just light enough to perceive a corpse is laid out.)
sp.p: there, will they behold the lifeless form of him, once the hope and delight of his family—here, at their feet a father, a sister, and mother, who will supplicate them to spare those precious relics, and not to cover with opprobrium his parent's remaining years. Should they be insensible to such a prayer, God himself will be offended!

div.stage: They form in a groupe, to receive a procession, which enters solemnly, Jacob first, shewing the way. Officer and Guards, with flambeaux. Apparitors, Goaler, Clerks. A Judge—the Capitoul in his Robes—a Judge. Two Surgeons Peace Officers and People with flambeaux.

They go shortly round—the Soldiers range across the Garden entrance at the back—the Capitoul and Judges in the center, the Officers, Clerks and Surgeons on one side—Peasantry on the other, and Ambroise at a particular moment glides in from the crowd—Madame Calas and Pauline kneel—Jacob, Laurence and Jeannette bend over them in an attitude of supplication— Edward supports the Ladies, and Calas stands in a firm but mournful manner pointing to the open door of the room where Antoine lies—Ambroise at some distance from him, also points significantly, and the Judges notice the mournful cabinet.—the Capitoul looks sternly around him upon all the groupe.

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: My Lord, we seek not to disguise the truth—my son is no more. I would have concealed his crime; nature and my love for him, would have made it a duty, nor do I think there is a father in the world would condemn me for it—you behold at your knees a family in despair, of whom the honour, and the fate is about to depend on your humanity.

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.p: Rise, Madame, rise—
You
ought to expect from magistrates, nothing but justice, and the punishment of crime.

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: Crime! is it not already expiated?

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.p: Society must be avenged—gentlemen
enter that apartment, examine the unfortunate who has ceased to live, and make your report conformable to truth—
sp.stage: (they go in and the door is closed, Madame Calas is following)
sp.p: —you Madame must remain—and you
deliver to those officers the keys of your house and of those places where your papers are enclosed.

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: How do they relate, my lord, to the event which brings you hither?

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.p: Obey, sir

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: My servant Jacob has been twenty years the depositary of my keys.

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.p: You have my instructions—accompany that man,
do you conduct him, and without reply or observation, do all he may command you.

sp.speaker: Jacob.
sp.p: Pardon me, your lordship—but in this house, I am accustomed to obey nobody's orders but those of my worthy master—if he commands, its quite another matter.

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: Yes, my friend—I order you to obey the magistrates.

sp.speaker: Jacob.
sp.p: Aye, aye, then indeed—this way.
sp.stage: (Sullenly to the Officers, and leads them off at the right hand door, two soldiers follow with torches; the clerks, &c., place seats and a table.)

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: What are your intentions, my lord? one would imagine by these formalities, we had been guilty of some culpable action.

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.stage: (receiving a folded paper from one of the other Judges.)
sp.p: You ought to know.
sp.stage: (seating himself, as do the others; Madame Calas sinks on a chair and hides her face, weeping; Pauline and Edward exchange anxious glances.)

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.p: Was not your son in the habit of passing much of his time from home?

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: Too much, my lord.

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.p: Was he from home, yesterday?

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: No, my lord.
sp.stage: (they copy his answers at the table.)

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.p: You received friends last night—what time did they retire.

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: About nine.

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.p: And at what hour did your son die?

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: Merciful powers? my son die! about that hour.

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.p: Were you then with your friends?

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: Yes—all the family—

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: No, my dear husband—you mistake—our son—was not with us.

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: True—my grief made me forget.

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.p: Observe how he contradicts himself.

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: Contradict himself! my lord, my lord, can a father overwhelm'd with agony, possess presence of mind sufficient to retain the most trivial circumstances of the frightful event which involved him in such affliction—do you imagine he would deceive you—what feelings could induce so evident an error?

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.p: You forget, sir, that I am the only person to ask questions here.

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: No, your lordship, my master is too much of a gentlemen to forget that he—

sp.speaker: Officer.
sp.p: Silence!

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.p: In what place did your son perish?

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: Yonder—in that pavilion.

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.p: What—in the very moment of reconciliation—after a quarrel you had had with your son—at the instant when you were close to the pavilion, conducting forth your company, your son, as it were, expires before your eyes, and you pretend ignorance of what was passing.
sp.stage: (Ambroise approaches and whispers to the Capitoul.)

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: Nothing can be more true, my lord.

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: The cries of our attendants first apprised us of the dreadful circumstance.

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: Mr. Edward! sir! madam! look— there's that—that Ambroise whispering with the judge.

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: Ambroise! what does he here? endeavour to inform my husband.

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: I will madam.—
sp.stage: (she steals round towards Calas, when Ambroise points her out to the Capitoul, who sternly addresses her.)

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.p: Whither are you going—

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: Going, my lord, I was going to—
sp.stage: (Madame Calas makes a sign to her.)

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.p: Let her speak, madam, Jeannette tell the truth.

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: The truth—to be sure my lord—I was going— I was—well, I was going to bid my master take care of himself.—

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.p: And why? dare not deceive.

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: Me—deceive—my lord—

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: My lord, Jeannette never deceived nobody in all her life, not even me—and—

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.p: Remove that fool—speak damsel—why was your master to take care of himself?

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: Because—why because that person there—Mr. Ambroise is here.

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.p: Very well.

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.p: You observe, my lord.
sp.stage: (the Surgeons re-enter, they present a paper to the Capitoul, who examines it and gives it to the other Judges.)

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.p: Gentlemen, we are of the same opinion—the circumstances you have remarked relative to the violent death of this young man, have been well considered.
There can be no doubt—what horror!
sp.stage: (looking severely at Calas—a general movement of surprise—Jacob, &c. re-enter—the Officers gives papers to the Capitoul.)

sp.speaker: Jacob.
sp.p: My dear master, they have ransacked every where, and took those papers from my dear young master's room.

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.p: Is this fragment of a letter your son's writing?

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: Yes, my lord, most certainly it is.

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.p: Hear then:
“Willingly would I fly to your arms—but what, upon the terms your family exact, would be the consequence?—I should draw upon myself the anger of my father, which would be the sentence of my death!”

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: Of his death!

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: He is lost!

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: My brother! oh, my brother! what evil thou hast done!

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: Do you comprehend this?

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: Suppose those are the words of my son—what mean they?

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.p: Since you persist in this affected ignorance, I must inform you, that all was prepared for his marriage with Hortensia, upon certain conditions, which you disapproved —the temple was illuminated, the altar was dressed, the priest attended—and—this fragment of a letter tells the rest.—You did not chuse the nuptials, under such circumstances, should take place.—It is proved, on the authority of these professional gentlemen, the, wounds your son received, could not be inflicted by himself, the question is, who gave them?

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: Almighty Providence!

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: Who gave them!

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.p: You!

div.stage: A general start of horror—Madame Calas falls into the chair she had quitted—a chord is struck by the orchestra, and a picture of strong effect of grief, anger, and surprise is formed.

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: Just Heaven! did I hear right—destroy my son!
Oh, Antoine! beloved of my heart:—arise—arise, I conjure you, and confront the daring false, and wicked accusers of thy broken hearted father!

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: And can so execrable a falsehood, find no baser issue, than from the mouth of a magistrate!

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: Barbarian! you!—a father! and dare imagine such a crime!

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.p: Wretch, we have a witness here—

sp.speaker: All.
sp.p: Ambroise!

sp.speaker: Calas & Edw.
sp.p: An impostor!

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: Aye, you may pull, and pinch, and wink, and nod, and cry silence, if you please, but I will speak now, if I never speak again—I know that person, I saw him come peeping through the gate—I was at first jealous of Jeannette, but little as I am, when I looked at his jesuitical leer, not so bad as that, thinks I, neither—and so I saw him creeping in again just as Mr. Calas came down out of the pavilion.

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.p: Mr. Calas came down out of the pavilion! a good witness—

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: To be sure I am—and Mr. Calas knows, as well as I do, all that happened there.

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: If, sir, it is true, you were the friend of my son, you ought to have pity on his unfortunate father, and proclaim the truth.

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.p: You shall hear it:—at nine o'clock I came to conduct your son to the altar, where he was expected; on my arrival, cries of distress and expressions of “murder and assassination,” assailed my ears—I saw Calas run from the pavilion, pale, disfigured—all seemed transfixed; and Madame, as if divining the crime her husband had committed, met him in well affected terror, and exclaimed—“my son is no more!”—overcome with horror, I fled this place of crime, believing that Heaven and man required me to denounce, what upon honor, I declare has taken place.

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: Monster!

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.p: What have you to answer?

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: Nothing, my lord.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: What, my father, have you nothing to reply to such a villain!—we are all witness you adored my brother.

sp.speaker: Jacob, Jean. & Lau.
sp.p: All, all, my lord, all!

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: My lord the Capitoul, it is impossible you can persist in so horrible an accusation—Nature forbids you, and you outrage Heaven in not resisting the foul charge—do you suppose men more ferocious than monsters?—The tyger cherishes his offspring, and do you think, a human father and mother, the most tender, the most respectable, could destroy the infant he had loved, and she had cherished at her bosom—What! cannot sixty years of virtue, kindness, and paternal example, guarantee from an action which reverses the order of nature—no—you do not yourselves believe it, can nor you find any other magistrates, who would admit the possibility of a similar outrage on nature and humanity.

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: Aye, my lord—hear him, and reject this horrible calumny.

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.p: Woman, thy speech becomes thee not.

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: True my lord, I am but woman—though long settled with my husband in a land of strangers, I have the honor to be an English woman—and in the dear land of my fathers, no one even when known to be guilty is pronounced so, until the accused is sentenced by an open and fair trial by his peers—by twelve impartial judges, who are neither friends nor enemies, my lord,

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.p: We must perform our duty—secure your prisoner, observe his family, and let the body of the son be conveyed to the place of trial.
Obey!

div.stage: Procession moves—Calas is surrounded by Guards.

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: My wife!—my daughter! need I express that I am innocent—courage! Heaven will not permit a just cause to perish—Edward—will you, dare you be my advocate?

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: I will justify or perish with the father of Pauline!

div.stage: The Procession goes on—the family of Calas surround him—Soldiers with flambeaux are just seen entering with the body of Antoine, covered with white drapery, Calas rushes out, Madame Calas falls senseless, the rest form a groupe, and the Act Drop slowly falls to a mournfully impressive sympathy.

div.head: Scene
div.stage: SCENE.

A grand Gothic Antichamber, at the back, a fine painted glass window looking into the main street, so that passengers &c. may be seen—on each side a lofty door— one inscribed “COUNCIL CHAMBER” the other “HALL OF JUSTICE”—Guards are at each—antique chairs, &c. furnish the hall.
Music. Enter Edward.

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: I have then pleaded his cause in vain; I see too well which way their thoughts are biased.

div.stage: Music. Ambroise enters from the Chamber of Justice, and is hastily crossing the stage, when he is stopped by Edward.

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: Stay, sir—I must speak with you—I insist.

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.p: By what authority?

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: You shall hear that, in spite of your wish to the contrary—here in the presence of all those witnesses— you shall escape no part of the truth, you shall avoid no part of the malediction of an innocent family whom you would drag to the scaffold.

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.p: Dare you, sir, prefer an accusation against me! do you know that this offence is equally directed against the majesty of that tribunal, whose sentence will quickly justify my conduct and repel your calumny.

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: And by what proofs will that tribunal give so horrible a sentence? if on your execrable accusation—if on your sacrilegious oath, it must be without consulting their consciences.—with a front of brass you swore before Heaven to tell the truth!—I saw the magistrates turn pale while you, without remorse, swore that the father had murdered his son under your observation—ah wretch!— if the thunder has not been launched aginst you, if the earth has not opened under your footsteps, acknowledge that clemency which yet gives you a respite to repent of your dreadful acts against the innocent.

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.p: You go too far—

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: Yet hear me—Calas is innocent, and you know it—what injuries has he done you?—I will repair them. I will yield to you all I possess, and keep your secret be what it may—you reflect—follow, without hesitation, the voice of your conscience, retract your guilty deposition, and arrest the arm of death ready to fall on a helpless good old man! The blood of the innocent will return upon your head, and will cry for retribution ou the terrible day of judgement—on the other hand be honest and I will overwhelm you with riches, I will spare you the terrors of crime, of remorse, and from the vengeance of your fellow men—come, come, let justice, let humanity triumph

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.p: And dare your hypocrisy propose this to me! if I return to the tribunal tremble for yourself, lest I should add to the honest proofs I have brought, the criminal and insulting offers you have had the audacity to make me.

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: Your heart then is inaccessible to remorse and to that feeling of terror which is experienced by the most daring.

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.p: I have nothing to dread; the Capitoul is convinced

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: Your art has known too well how to mislead him.

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.p: Dare you accuse the premier magistrate?

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: I accuse none but you—and that before my God! since nothing can stay your crime, since, in your blind rage you see nothing but the abyss into which you would plunge Calas; hasten, wretch, and accomplish thy dastardly, thy fell intention! but hear the oath which I swear—if the father of my betrothed thro' thy accursed perjury should be doom'd to mount the scaffold, the very bowels of the earth will not hide thee from my vengeance, and thy blood, yes, thine, traitor, thy blood shall answer me for his.

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.p: Imprudent! daring man! I hasten to denounce you.

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: Denounce me! so thou shalt—Villain, I'll drag thee to the judgement seat.

div.stage: Enter Officer. Jacob, Jeannette and Guards.

sp.speaker: Officer.
sp.p: Clear the entrances—the debates are finished, and the judges are retiring to the council chamber.

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: It is over then, and sentence is about to be pronounced —dost thou not tremble villain?

sp.speaker: Jacob.
sp.p: Friend! Mr. Edward—how do they proceed?

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: O say—tell us—

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: They are going to debate upon the sentence,

sp.speaker: Jacob.
sp.p: Sentence, O Heaven!

div.stage: Music.

Soldiery, &c. cross and form on a platform which leads from the hall of justice to the council chamber, people also enter but are kept just between the wings by the muskets and halberds of the guards—Madame Calas and Pauline enter in front.—Ambroise tries to escape up the steps towards the judgement hall, but is put back by the officer of the guards.

sp.speaker: Officer.
sp.p: No one passes till the judges leave the hall.

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: Dear Madame! whither would you go?

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: Whither! Ah Edward, my friend! my husband is about to be condemned—condemned! no! 'tis impossible! behold his judges!—join with me, let us throw ourselves at their feet and implore their clemency.

div.stage: The grand officers of the court, &c pass across the platform from the hall of justice towards the council chamber, in front of the guards, who present arms when the Capitoul is in the center, the Music stops, and Mde. Calas exclaims—

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: Stay! stop! hold! for the love of Heaven!

sp.speaker: Jacob & Jean.
sp.p: Mercy! mercy! for our beloved master!

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.p: What would you, madam?

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: My husband is innocent—we swear by all that is most sacred; in the name of that power which must one day judge yourselves, do not consummate so horrible an injustice—do not credit the testimony of a monster, an impostor, when opposed to the protestation of the best, the most respectable of husbands, fathers, and of men.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: Save, oh, save my father!

sp.speaker: Jean. & Jacob.
sp.p: Mercy! mercy!

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.p: Rise, madame:—gentlemen, on to the council chamber.

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: Cruel! obdurate men!

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.p: Nor tears, nor menaces, can now avail: our opinions are formed, and nothing ought to change them—I permit the accused, during our deliberations, to see you and any of his friends in this hall:—on gentlemen.

div.stage: The Capitoul and Judges pass on to the council chamber, the guards and people keep their stations.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: We shall see him then—dearest mother, let us yet hope the best.

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.p: I may now escape unnoticed.

div.stage: Jacob, who had been looking in at the hall, intercepts him.)

sp.speaker: Jacob.
sp.p: Ambroise!

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: Art thou yet here? hast thou the audacity to face thy victims?

div.stage: (Ambroise stands as if petrified.)

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: Execrable calumniator! comest thou to satiate thyself in my husband's blood! what injury has he done thee, or I, or this innocent maid, who will soon be fatherless?—from what demon art thou sent to exterminate an unoffending family?

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.p: Madame—

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: Thou alone art his accuser, thou alone would drag him to the scaffold,—it is on thy head alone his blood will fall—while our sorrows, our maledictions, and the thunders of insulted heaven will pursue you to the tomb!

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.p: Away—let me depart!

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: No—your punishment is doomed to commence with the suffering of your victim—but his, will soon finish in celestial triumph, while your's will continue without an end.—Remorse will unceasingly pursue you, by day and by night, and when thy sickening soul is permitted to shut out this mortal light, thine eyes will but re-open to renewed punishment in the world hereafter.

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: Hear'st thou, wretch!

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: Malediction! malediction!

sp.speaker: All.
sp.p: Malediction!!

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.p: What, oh! help!—'tis insupportable—furies loose your grasp—I will be free of ye—

div.stage: Runs desperately up the steps of the hall of justice— meets Calas, starts, staggers back hides his face, and is caught in the arms of the guards, who take him off Calas runs and embraces his family, who form a momentary picture.

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: Thus surrounded by thee,

by my children, for thou art one of them, dear Edward—by my friends, for so my servants still have been.—I can for a moment, forget we have ever been unhappy—you weep— ah, too well I feel, that if it is hard on me, thus to be taken from ye, how much more painful to you, who are in such a world, to be left behind.

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: Do not believe I will support it—no—happy have we lived together, and now I follow thee to death—

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: What say'st thou!—and our daughter! is it not enough, that in one day, she should lose brother, father, husband—but thou wou'd'st also take a mother from her!—oh, no—thou must remain.

sp.speaker: Jacob.
sp.p: And we too, dear master; my daughter and myself will serve our dear ladies, on our knees will serve them, now ten times more respectable from the misery they suffer.

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: And did you say, my father, that your daughter was about to lose the husband of her choice?

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: I know your heart—Edward—I know its feelings —but your father was my dearest friend, and should I be doom'd to suffer public execution, I cannot consent that his son should, by such an alliance, become a sharer in the infamy of my injured family.

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: Infamy is for crime, not for innocence—the name of Calas will be ennobled by misfortune, and I shall be most proud to share its reputation. If they take your fortune, mine remains for these, and your virtues will be the splendid inheritance they bring me in return—for me, I will for ever protest your innocence and proclaim it to the world at the peril of my life—here in the awful moment while your judges are debating whether they shall consign, not you, but themselves, to disgrace or honour— now give me the hand of your daughter and let your virtuous benediction be the certain gaurrantee of our future happiness.

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: Excellent.

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: My wife—assist me to join them, and, O my children, may Heaven accept the vows of my heart, and may my sufferings, endured and offered with resignation, call down on you the blessings you so well deserve.

div.stage: Enter Laurence and Officer.

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: What—refuse to let see him—I tell you I'm one of the family, every body knows it—ha my name's Laurence, valet and gardener to Mr. Counsellor Edward, and going to be married as soon as possible, to ma'amselle Jeannette, daughter of old Jacob, and waiting maid to her own young mistress—only ask, if you won't believe.

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: Laurence! yes, he belongs to me—

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: And to me too, with submission, sir.

sp.speaker: Offi.
sp.p: Pass then.

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: Justice indeed—I'm sure justice is the most unjustest impolitest, un---

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: Peace, bring you any news?

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: News! bless you—why I said you didn't know it—how should you—but hush—Ah, Monsieur Calas—if you knew what's going on in the town you'd bless yourself, but may one speak?

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: Yes, but softly.

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: Then there's a most glorious rumpus—such junketty poodle—big, little, rich, poor, tag rag, and rory boys, all declare they'll sooner hang up the Capitoul himself, than he shall lay finger on an innocent man, that's not guilty of no crime of any kind.

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: Now fate forbid.

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: They won't be forbid—all the workmen, the shop keepers, the every body, they call you their father, friend and benefactor—they swear they'll set fire to the town if a hair of your head is but once touch'd, and things come to that, I could find in my own heart to be one among the jolly conflagrationarians.

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: Shew me! lead me—I have in vain defonded you before the judges, and now—

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: Edward! remain! I conjure—I command you—should my judges erroneously condemn me to the wheel, they only will destroy this worthless body, which if you dare to rescue by a violation of the laws, you, more cruel than their sentence, will become the assassin of my family, the executioner of my reputation.

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: The wheel said you! I shall spare your judges a a dreadful crime, are you not innocent and the father of my wife?

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: O husband! save my father!

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: Son! preserve my dying husband!

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: Stay, Edward, stay—
alas! he's lost, he's lost!

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: Not while I can find him, and if he must be lost it shan't be by himself, while I've a leg to stand on.

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: What have you done?—fly—bring him back, and you, my daughter, consider he is your husband, and 'tis your duty to save him when he would rush upon his ruin.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: My first duty is to save my father—my heart trembles for Edward, but to snatch you from a cruel death, I could sacrifice him and myself.

sp.speaker: Jacob
sp.p: The judges are returning to make report.

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: My blood runs cold.

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: My fate is fixed—I shall have no more trials to sustain, and have only to submit me to the will of Heaven!

div.stage: The Judges re-enter from the council chamber—the Capitoul gives written orders to an officer, and the soldiers are directed different ways.

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: What mean those dreadful orders—those arrangements?

sp.speaker: Cap
sp.p: I recommend you madam, and your daughter, in the name of the council, to retire.
sp.stage: (they look at the Capitoul, and approach Calas still nearer, as if fearful of quitting him.)
sp.p: You have heard me, will you not have the goodness to obey?

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: No, my lord, my daughter and I—will— will remain—I will never abandon my husband—I am as he is, equally innocent or guilty—our actions have been the same, nothing ought to divide our fate—if you condemn him, all his family are willing to march with him to the place of execution and be partakers of his punishment —my daughter, your father and ourselves are one—
My lord judge, we are here, we are ready—pronounce your award, and let the same blow fall upon us all.

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: My lord! do you hear them!

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.p: Do you persist in denying that you have accomplices.

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: Where no crime exists, how can there be accomplices?

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.p: And thus you reject by a culpable silence, the clemency of Heaven and the indulgence of man.

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: On the contrary, I implore both—for the most innocent has need of them—and do you, my lord, consider that Heaven beholds, and will judge you equally with myself.

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.p: Listen to your sentence.

div.stage: Music—he takes a paper from one of the other Judges and opens it with hesitation—Calas attends with his eyes raised toward heaven, the ladies keep close to him. Jacob and Jeannette hang on each other in fearful expectation, at a little distance.

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: O God! thou knowest his innocence—avert this evil from him.

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.p: “The tribunal assembled to enquire into the murder of Marc Antoine Calas, have, on the testimony of the witness Ambroise, and other corroborating circumstances, resolved that the said crime could only have been committed by John Calas, who, by a majority of seven voices to five, is hereby condemned to the pain of death.”
sp.stage: (all droop round Calas, who alone remains firm and erect.)

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: Husband!

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: Father!

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.p: “And in consequence of a threatened opposition to this sentence, it is ordered to be carried into instant execution,”
“and that the magistrates shall not quit their posts till the the third sound of the great bell shall announce the death of the condemned.”
Officers, see that the decision of the tribunal be effected.

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: Can it be true?—I follow thee to death— nothing shall separate us, and the executioners shall only strike thee through this bosom!

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: Where then is your fortitude—your noble and pious resignation? when we have now to fulfil the highest, the most sublime duties the Eternal has prescribed to man! let my death and thy life serve as examples, while I join my son, and prepare thy place in another and a happier world.

div.stage: (an Officer signs to the Capitoul that all is ready.

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.p: We have delay'd too long.

div.stage: The Guards divide at the back, the great central window opens and a scaffold hung with black and surrounded with Soldiers, is seen—a wheel is elevated—the bell strikes Once—the family, with a suppressed shriek, hide their eyes, and cling close to Calas.

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: Farewell! my friends! my child! my good, my faithful wife! may Heaven love and protect you better than I have done—tell Edward I forbid him to revenge my fall. I forgive my enemies—and—my Judges—may God forgive them as I do. Pauline—support your mother— adieu! adieu!

div.stage: Madame Calas falls into the arms of those about her— Calas kisses her—the bell tolls a second time—he tears himself from her—the Guards point to the scaffold.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: Mother! mother! they take him from us!

sp.speaker: Mde Calas.
sp.p: Hold! hold!

sp.speaker: Calas.
sp.p: In the name of Heaven, shorten my sufferings!

div.stage: He rushes out through the central window, which is closed after him—the Judges return into the chamber of justice—Jacob follows his master—Madame Calas sinks on a sort of bench—Pauline falls at her feet, hiding her face in her mother's lap—Jeannette stands behind sobbing, with her apron to her eyes—Ambroise enters, and is passing out, when the groupe of the three females arrests his attention.

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.p: Behold my work!—I have satisfied my hatred—I have consummated my vengeance, and now—aye—now the crime begins to reward itself.

div.stage: Enter Gilbert with a Letter.

sp.speaker: Gil.
sp.p: At last I have got through the crowd: since seven this morning have I been trying to—ah! dear, dear! sure enough that is the poor suffering family!—poor—dear—
What a damned villain must the fellow be, who has brought them to this misery!
sp.stage: (Ambroise starts—Gilbert nearly runs against him.—During this, Pauline and Jeannette busy themselves to recover Mde. Calas.)
sp.p: I beg your pardon, sir; perhaps you can be my friend—I have got a letter here of some consequence—'tis for the Capitoul, the premier Judge.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: She'll never revive.

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: And no one to help us!

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.p: For the Capitoul! let's see—let's see—by all that's terrible—'tis—yes, 'tis the hand writing of—

sp.speaker: Gil.
sp.p: You know the writing then?

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.p: The writing!—why—at what hour did you receive this?

sp.speaker: Gil.
sp.p: At—at eight last night.

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.p: And where?

sp.speaker: Gil.
sp.p: Close by the house of Monsieur Calas.

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.p: My friend—you—you cannot see the Capitoul.

sp.speaker: Gil.
sp.p: Not see him!

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.p: Not at present—but I'll undertake—he—he shall have it—when the—the business of the day is ended

sp.speaker: Gil.
sp.p: No! will you? how good you are—you must feel for those poor people—its a sad thing to have committed a crime!—but such men as you—for I know you, sir— such men as you, who are kind and condescending, and never have injured nobody—you are paid by—

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.p: Yes, yes, but—

sp.speaker: Gil.
sp.p: Your own feelings—I dare say, they speak much more than I can do—poor family! I thank you kindly, sir.—Do let me help.

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.p: Go! go! my punishment indeed, begins.

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.stage: (as the people clear away from Madame Calas.)
sp.p: She breathes—she opens her eyes—ah! my mother!

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: Madame! dear madame!

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.p: Let us see— let us see—
sp.stage: (they lead Madame Calas up the stage.)

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.p: How fortunate!—by hell! had I not seen this, I had been lost for ever—this witness must be destroyed—

div.stage: As he is going to tear it, an Officer from the chamber of justice, lays his hand on his arm.

sp.speaker: Officer.
sp.p: My lord the Capitoul, would see you, sir.

sp.speaker: Amb
sp.p: The Capitoul!

sp.speaker: Offi.
sp.p: He has ordered me, to conduct you to his presence.

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.p: I follow you—this—this—
shall never appear.
sp.stage: (exit with the Officer into the hall of justice.)

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: What darkness surrounds me—
where is my son!—where is my husband! am I then alone!
sp.stage: Goes slowly and wildly round the stage, as if searching for some one—Pauline and Jeannette unable to attend longer to her—weep, leaning on each other—Madame Calas at length, reads the inscriptions over the two doors, and exclaims in a hollow tone—
sp.p: A hall of justice—chamber of council—ah!
My husband is gone to death!!
sp.stage: (is rushing out, and stopped by her daughter and Jeannette.)

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: Mother!

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: Madam!

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: Come, come, come, my friend—come my child—let us die with him—come— come—

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: Dear madam, do not, do not go!
hark! 'tis Mr. Edward—Edward, madame, and my father —perhaps some hope—

div.stage: Enter Edward, Jacob and People.
Edward dragging on Gilbert—the women run to him.

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: My husband! where?

sp.speaker: Paul.
sp.p: My father!

sp.speaker: Jean.
sp.p: My master!

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: Perhaps I bring his justification—his safety—a letter from your son Antoine.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.p: A letter!!

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: Where is the man you gave it to—where is he—where is he? speak—

sp.speaker: Gil.
sp.p: I don't know—he was here—Patience —he's gone to give it to the Capitoul.

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: Let us fly
sp.stage: (rushes into the hall of justice, followed by the people, &c.)

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: My child!—my friend! what an awful moment!

div.stage: Enter the Capitoul, Judges, &c. &c.

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.p: What tumult!—

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.stage: (holding Gilbert, and pointing to those who enter.)
sp.p: Observe—is that the man to whom you gave the letter— or was it him—or him?

sp.speaker: Gil.
sp.p: No!

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: Him?

sp.speaker: Gil.
sp.p: No!

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: I tremble—

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: Take heed—

sp.speaker: Gil.
sp.p: No, no—
there! that's he— that's he—the good worthy—yes, that's the man I gave the letter to—

sp.speaker: The Family.
sp.p: Ambroise!!

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.p: What means this?

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: The traitor possesses a letter, addressed to you—tis from the son of Calas, and may announce the innocence of his father.

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.p: Me!—

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.p: A letter!

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: Order them to take it from him, or by all that's good I'll render you responsible for the death of the innocent.

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.p: Take it from him.

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: Hasten—my husband is on his way to death.

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.stage: (siezes the letter, and holds it up.)
sp.p: Tis here!— tis here!

sp.speaker: All.
sp.p: Tis here! here, my lord
sp.stage: (they give the letter to the Capitoul.)

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.p: “Let no one be accused of my death—Ambroise, Ambroise alone conducted me to the precipice—and the blow which extricates me is given by myself.”—Wretch!

sp.speaker: Mde. Calas.
sp.p: Haste! save my husband!

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.p: Run! fly!

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: Let me be the first!

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.p: I am lost!!

div.stage: As they go out, a third sound of the bell is heard, all form a picture of affright—the Capitoul staggers, and falls on the seat, where Madame Calas had fainted— the Guards surround Ambroise.

sp.speaker: Jacob, &c.
sp.p: He's lost!

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: He would have been—but I'm in time!
sp.stage: (a grand shout—Calas appears at the window—the family rush towards him.)
sp.p: Had he died, that mournful bell would for ever have sounded in your ears.—Ages to come would have done him justice, and the name of Calas would have been written in characters of blood!

div.stage: Ambroise endeavouring to escape, is surrounded by the soldiery, with uplifted swords—groupes are formed all over the stage.

sp.speaker: Edw.
sp.p: Thus may innocence triumph, and villainy meet its just reward!
